description: I'm a 3rd year BSc Physics student along with tech interest. We'll turn NASA's microgravity combustion data into AI-driven fire safety insights. I'll cover physics interpretation, data cleaning, and whatever else is needed. Looking for: a Python/ML coder, a data visualization person, and writer/presenter. All skill levels welcome. Virtual, steady pace.
summary:
Flame in Free Fall is a web app that brings 15 NASA microgravity fire safety experiments into one place. Users pick a place (Earth, ISS, Moon base or Spacesuit) or an oxygen level and a material, then see which experiments covered it. The app ranks experiments and compares them side by side with a transparent confidence score. It also maps where oxygen and airflow have never been tested together. Ask SI, an AI assistant, answers questions only from our sourced data. It cites a link for every fact and says “No proof in our data” when evidence is missing.

It addresses the challenge by turning scattered results into something people can search, compare and trust, and by showing the gaps instead of hiding them. Our main finding is that all 9 untested zones sit at 25% oxygen or more with airflow of 10 cm/s or more. This matters because future habitats and spacesuits may use higher oxygen levels, and knowing what is untested tells researchers which experiment to run next.
details:
Overview

Flame in Free Fall is a web application that consolidates all 15 of the fire safety microgravity experiments conducted by NASA. You select where you want to test (Earth, ISS, Moon base, Spacesuit), select an oxygen level and material and the application will tell you which experiments were covered. Then using a simplistic formula (oxygen, airflow and material) the experiments are ranked. They can be compared using the confidence score, the higher the confidence score the better sourced and detailed the information is. The gap map illustrates where there are no experiments for certain oxygen and airflow levels. The Ask SI feature provides answers to your questions using only our cleaned dataset. This includes a source link for every single fact. If there was not enough evidence to provide an answer it will say ‘No proof in our data’.

Benefits

The benefits are that researchers and students can quickly search, compare and trust the fire experiments. Our key finding was that all 9 areas with no experiments were either 25% oxygen or higher and had an airflow of 10cm/s or higher. Our aim is to help teams plan their next experiments.

Technologies

The application and charts were made using Python, Streamlit, pandas and Altair. The Ask SI feature was created using the Groq API (openai/gpt-oss-120b). We used GitHub for our code and Streamlit Community Cloud to host. No specific hardware was required.

Creativity

Most tools only show us what we know. Using this tool we can see what we don’t know. The gap map, next experiment suggestions and Earth uses page showing our data, general knowledge and unknowns in different sections with labels, means we can see the limitations of the evidence.

Considerations

We wanted to ensure that everything was trustworthy and honest. All numbers have a source link. All scores show what formula they have used. We have clearly labelled our choices, such as Moon base and Spacesuit are our names for the atmospheres matched to NASA, which are 26.5% and 34% oxygen. We have also listed experiments with no oxygen data. The AI has been very limited so it can’t make up facts.
